title: Out-of-tune pianos, the Rhodes and the Yamaha electric piano
summary: Pianos are poorly kept; he finds the Rhodes decent and a Yamaha closest to acoustic.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: When you were jobbing around, did you confront a piano that was so far down that you had to play the whole night a half tone up?

Yeah; right, that's happened a lot of times. Pianos aren't cared for very well in this country. In most commercial places they don't keep them up, they don't have them tuned, they let them go down and they go down and down.
Did you ever run into a gig where you had to play a piano with the little buttons on it, that all sounded like a nickelodeon?
No, I've never come across that.
Some of the old pianos had little steel discs that dropped down in front of the hammers.
I've come across some pretty funky pianos.
This was a stylistic thing back in the twenties and thirties, and of course they survived for a long time.
All of this is why, no matter how bad a Rhodes seems to fit, at least the keys work and it's kind of good. Do you play a Rhodes now? Do you like a Rhodes?

Of those type of pianos I think the Rhodes has the best sound I've come across, until recently. The hotel that I'm working at now picked up a Yamaha that has strings; it's an electric piano but it sounds very close to an acoustic piano. That's the claim to fame that this particular Yamaha piano has, well thought of in the profession.

I'd say that as far as electronic pianos are concerned, and generally speaking I don't like an electronic piano, this particular Yamaha is the closest to the real piano that I've encountered. It really reproduces the sound, especially in the middle register, very akin to an acoustic piano. Upper register tends to become bell like and the lower register tends to be very fuzzy.
